common_name: Daebong Persimmon (Korean Heart-Shaped Giant Astringent Persimmon)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun once frost danger has passed, giving it room to grow into a large, vigorous specimen.

directions: Daebong is one of Korea's most widely grown astringent persimmon cultivars, prized for its oversized, heart-shaped fruit with deep orange skin and flesh. Like other astringent-type kaki, the fruit must be fully softened or treated to remove tannins before it becomes palatable, at which point it develops a rich, honeyed sweetness eaten with a spoon rather than bitten into firm. The tree is vigorous and productive, and because it is self-fruitful a single tree can set a full crop without a separate pollinator nearby. Give it the same full-sun, well-drained siting as other Asian persimmons and expect fruit to color in mid to late autumn.
sources: National Center for Biotechnology Information (PubMed Central)

common_name: Cheongdo Bansi Persimmon (Korean Flat Seedless Astringent Persimmon)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun; Bansi stays notably smaller than most kaki cultivars, so it suits home orchards with limited space.

directions: Bansi is the signature persimmon of Cheongdo County in South Korea, named for its flattened, disc-like shape, and it is unusual among astringent kaki cultivars for reliably setting fruit with no seeds. Growers in the region attribute the seedlessness to local climate conditions that favor female flower development, since the same scion grown elsewhere typically produces seeded fruit. Like other astringent types, the orange-skinned fruit carries high tannin levels until fully ripened or deliberately deastringed, after which the flesh turns soft and very sweet. It is grown both for fresh eating once softened and for slicing into dried persimmon, a regional specialty product of Cheongdo.

common_name: Yotsumizo Persimmon (Japanese Grooved Astringent Drying Persimmon)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun with good drainage, giving it standard Asian persimmon spacing to mature into a full-sized tree.

directions: Yotsumizo is a traditional Japanese astringent persimmon whose name refers to the four shallow longitudinal grooves that mark its fruit, giving it a distinctive faceted look compared to the smoother rounded shapes of cultivars like Hachiya. Because it is a fully astringent type, fruit needs to be either fully bletted, CO2-treated, or dried before eating to break down its tannin content. It is among the cultivars traditionally favored in Japan for hoshigaki-style hot-air drying, where the firm flesh holds up well through the drying process. As with other kaki, plant it in full sun with good drainage and expect harvest in mid to late autumn.
sources: Growables.org (Julia F. Morton, Fruits of Warm Climates)

common_name: Luotian Tianshi Persimmon (Chinese Non-Astringent Flat Persimmon)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun; this late-ripening cultivar benefits from the longest possible warm season to finish naturally losing its astringency before harvest.

directions: Luotian Tianshi, originating in Hubei Province, is notable as the sole non-astringent persimmon cultivar of Chinese origin, meaning its fruit naturally loses astringency on the tree well before full ripeness and can be eaten firm and crisp like an apple without any bletting or artificial treatment. Its flattened, yellowish-orange fruit carries many seeds and ripens later in the season than most non-astringent Japanese cultivars. Because its natural deastringency trait is genetically dominant, breeding programs around the world have used it as parent germplasm to develop new non-astringent persimmon selections. Grow it with the same full-sun, well-drained conditions as other kaki cultivars, and allow the long growing season it needs to fully color and sweeten before picking.
sources: Journal of the Japanese Society for Horticultural Science
